a1.all.label: fact

items.text: Cerulli states that for the past decade, financial firms have shifted their compensation models from largely commission-based to an asset-related fee structure.
items.quote: For the past decade, financial firms have shifted their compensation models from largely commission-based to an asset-related fee structure.

items.text: Cerulli attributes the increased willingness of affluent investors to pay for advice in part to continued fee compression across both advisors and product fees.
items.quote: This 30-percentage-point increase can be attributed in part to greater accessibility of financial advice, continued fee compression across both advisors and product fees, and the proliferation of fiduciary advice

items.text: McKinsey/PriceMetrix states that after a period of fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013 to 2018, fee rates have stabilized, and increasing demand for human advice is a factor behind stable to slightly increasing advisory fee rates across delivery models.
items.quote: After a period of fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013to 2018, fee rates havestabilized, according to PriceMetrix by McKinsey.

items.text: McKinsey/PriceMetrix states fee rates for $1.0 million to $1.5 million advisory relationships have stayed at an average of approximately 104 basis points since 2019.
items.quote: fee rates for $1.0million to $1.5million advisory relationships havestayed at anaverageof approximately 104basis points since 2019.

items.text: McKinsey states fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019.
items.quote: Historically, fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019

items.text: McKinsey believes fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.
items.quote: We believe fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.

items.text: Deloitte states lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing, while competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare.
items.quote: Lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing. At the same time, competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare.

items.text: Raymond James states regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins.
items.quote: In fixed income and equity markets, regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins.

items.text: Raymond James believes price competition and pricing pressures in these and other areas will continue as institutional investors reduce the amounts they are willing to pay.
items.quote: We believe that price competition and pricing pressures in these and other areas will continue as institutional investors continue to reduce the amounts they are willing to pay

items.text: Raymond James CEO Paul Shoukry says advisors have been shifting their business over a long period of time to more fee-based and advisory-based relationships.
items.quote: advisors over a long period of time have been shifting their business to more fee-based business and advisory-based relationships.

items.text: Raymond James CEO Paul Shoukry says the firm would be flexible and open to evolving its pricing fees and payout if the industry evolves based on competitive pressures and client preferences.
items.quote: if that evolves in the industry based on competitive pressures and competitive dynamics and client preferences, most importantly, then of course, we would be flexible and open to evolving with where clients and advisers in the industry is evolving to. I mean we look at that on an ongoing basis for all of our pricing fees and payout.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it continues to experience price competition in some of its businesses, and says electronic execution and new technologies will likely continue the pressure on revenues.
items.quote: We continue to experience price competition in some of our businesses. In particular, the ability to execute securities, derivatives and other financial instrument trades electronically on exchanges, swap execution facilities and other automated trading platforms, and the introduction and application of new technologies, including generative artificial intelligence and tokenization, will likely continue the pressure on revenues.

items.text: Bank of America states increased competition may reduce fee-based revenue through pricing pressure, and that non-traditional providers now offer electronic securities trading with low or no fees and commissions.
items.quote: Increased competition may reduce our market share, net interest margin and fee-based revenue and negatively affect our results of operations, including through pricing pressure

a1.all.reason: Passages state the industry direction on fee models, fee levels, and fee compression.

a2.all.label: fact

items.text: Raymond James states regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins.
items.quote: In fixed income and equity markets, regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins.

items.text: Raymond James states Form CRS requires broker-dealers and investment advisers to provide retail investors a brief summary document with simple, easy-to-understand information about the relationship, and that its implementation resulted in additional client disclosures.
items.quote: Form CRS requires that broker-dealers and investment advisers provide retail investors with a brief summary document containing simple, easy-to-understand information about the nature of the relationship between the parties.

items.text: Edward Jones states the SEC rule requires registered investment advisers and broker-dealers to deliver a Form CRS Relationship Summary to clients informing them of fees, costs, conflicts of interest, and legal and disciplinary history.
items.quote: the SEC rule requiring registered investment advisers and broker-dealers to deliver a Form CRS Relationship Summary to their clients informing them of the types of client relationships offered, together with the applicable standards of care, and information on fees, costs, conflicts of interest, and legal and disciplinary history.

items.text: Wealthtender research finds fee transparency is the highest-impact priority for financial professionals, at 73%, and advises ensuring pricing is clearly communicated.
items.quote: Fee transparency (73% priority) – ensure your pricing is clearly communicated across all marketing materials

items.text: Wealthtender research finds nearly half of survey participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors leading them to choose one advisor over another.
items.quote: Nearly half of survey participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors that lead them to choose one advisor over others.

items.text: Wealthtender research finds just over 38% of people consider lack of transparency about fees or commissions a major red flag.
items.quote: Just over 38% of people consider lack of transparency about fees or commissions a major red flag.

items.text: McKinsey believes fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.
items.quote: We believe fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.

items.text: Deloitte states that as AI shows up in the service experience, the differentiators for advisers will be trust, transparency, and accountability.
items.quote: Advisers will still be the face of the firm, so the differentiators will be trust, transparency, and accountability, especially as AI shows up in the service experience.

items.text: InvestmentNews reports the broader debate over cash sweep transparency and pricing remains a live issue, with the SEC's sustained focus on sweep disclosures and litigation over allegedly low client yields, meaning the question is unlikely to fade.
items.quote: the broader debate over cash sweep transparency and pricing remains a live issue. The SEC's sustained focus on sweep disclosures, combined with a wave of litigation against major firms over allegedly low client yields, means that the question of who benefits from rising rates on uninvested cash is unlikely to fade from client conversations any time soon.

items.text: FINRA's report identifies providing clear disclosure on account type recommendations, giving retail customers clear, accessible materials to compare features, benefits and costs, as an effective practice.
items.quote: Providing Clear Disclosure on Account Type Recommendations: Providing retail customers with clear, accessible materials that allow them to compare the features, benefits and costs of certain account type recommendations (e.g., rollovers).

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it is required under ERISA Section 408(b)(2) regulations to provide information regarding its services and compensation so fiduciaries and plan sponsors can assess the reasonableness of its compensation.
items.quote: In accordance with Department of Labor regulations under Section 408(b)(2) of ERISA, MSWM is required to provide certain information regarding our services and compensation to assist fiduciaries and plan sponsors

items.text: Charles Schwab states it is required under the Advisers Act to provide clients with disclosure brochures describing its services, the fees charged, and important conflicts of interest.
items.quote: Charles Schwab & Co., Inc. ('CS&Co.') is required under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (the 'Advisers Act') to provide clients with disclosure brochures that describe our investment advisory and financial planning services, including how these services work, the fees charged, and important conflicts of interest.

a7.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones management describes targeting "Next Generation investors" through a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining them.
items.quote: and a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors

items.text: Management describes the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer as including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values.
items.quote: The Partnership's continued ability to compete and adapt its business model may be adversely impacted by the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values.

a7.EDJ.reason: Passages show how management frames Next Generation investors and changing client demographics and needs.

a8.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones discloses a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors among its client-targeting initiatives.
items.quote: and a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors

items.text: Edward Jones serves clients through its branch teams and offers investment advisory programs, brokerage and retirement accounts, cash and lending solutions, and financial planning offerings (general offerings, not specific to younger investors).
items.quote: The Partnership offers a variety of different solutions to clients, including investment advisory programs, brokerage and retirement accounts, cash and lending solutions and financial planning offerings.

items.text: Edward Jones' Digital and Data division supports technology infrastructure and digital initiatives to provide new tools for branch teams to better serve clients (general capability, not specific to younger investors).
items.quote: The Partnership's Digital and Data division supports the significant investment in technology infrastructure and digital initiatives to provide new tools for branch teams to better serve clients, enhance the operational support the home office provides to the branch teams and create operational efficiencies that reduce manual processes.

items.text: Edward Jones announced a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken, intended as a step toward integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities into Edward Jones to support advisor conversations with clients.
items.quote: Edward Jones announced that they have taken a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken , with an explicit intention that the investment is a step towards integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities more directly into Edward Jones as a way to support their value proposition and advisor conversations with clients.

a8.EDJ.reason: Passages describe current offerings, digital capabilities, and a personal finance app capability relevant to younger investors.

a9.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones states it is targeting new clients through a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.
items.quote: and a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors

items.text: Edward Jones lists among its aspirations to attract and serve new client segments.
items.quote: Attract and serve new client segments

items.text: Edward Jones aspires to anticipate clients' needs with the right offering at the right time, now and for generations to come.
items.quote: Anticipate clients' needs with the right offering at the right time, now and for generations to come

items.text: Edward Jones aspires to continue investing in technology to scale its ability to provide financial planning to clients.
items.quote: Continue investing in technology to scale our ability to provide financial planning to our clients

a9.EDJ.reason: Passages state priorities to attract new client segments including Next Generation investors and invest in technology.

a10.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones names competition from firms providing enhanced digital experiences, including AI and lower-cost computer-based robo-advice (competition named generally, not specifically tied to younger investors).
items.quote: with an increasing number of firms of all sizes providing enhanced digital experiences for clients, including the utilization of artificial intelligence technologies and lower cost, computer-based "robo-advice."

items.text: Edward Jones names competition from fintech companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms (competition named generally, not specifically tied to younger investors).
items.quote: The Partnership also faces competition from "fintech" companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms.

items.text: Edward Jones names competition from robo-advisors, other lower cost options, and fintech companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms (competition named generally, not specifically tied to younger investors).
items.quote: The Partnership is also subject to competition in the industry from robo-advisors and other lower cost options and from "fintech" companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms and from other non-traditional competitors.

items.text: Edward Jones names competition from major competitor brokerage firms that offer zero commissions for purchases and sales of stocks, ETFs and other brokerage products (competition named generally, not specifically tied to younger investors).
items.quote: including major competitor brokerage firms that offer zero commissions for purchases and sales of stocks, ETFs and other brokerage products

a10.EDJ.reason: Passages name digital, mobile, robo-advice, and zero-commission competitors, though not explicitly tied to younger investors.

a11.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones attributes a downward trend in net new assets to higher asset outflows influenced by an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm, among other factors.
items.quote: These outflows are impacted by a variety of factors, including, without limitation, an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm, macroeconomic volatility, inflation and consumer spending.

items.text: Edward Jones says year-to-date net new asset outflows continue an increasing downward trend influenced by an aging client base, generational wealth transfers outside the firm, and other factors.
items.quote: The outflows relative to the prior-year period continue an increasing downward trend influenced by several factors, including an aging client base, generational wealth transfers outside the firm, macroeconomic volatility, inflationary pressures, and shifts in consumer spending.

a11.EDJ.reason: Passages state Edward Jones is losing assets through generational wealth transfers outside the firm, relevant to younger heirs.

a12.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones discloses a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors, part of initiatives including potential future solutions in development and recently launched products.
items.quote: and a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors

items.text: In August 2026, Edward Jones announced it took a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken as a step toward integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities into Edward Jones.
items.quote: Edward Jones announced that they have taken a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken , with an explicit intention that the investment is a step towards integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities more directly into Edward Jones as a way to support their value proposition and advisor conversations with clients.

items.text: Edward Jones notes it is still determining the actual deployment strategy for Quicken, including where or how it will be offered to clients and integrated into internal advisor software.
items.quote: Edward Jones itself notes that they are still determining the actual deployment strategy , to decide where or how Quicken will be offered to their clients and integrated into their internal advisor software platforms.

a12.EDJ.reason: Passages disclose a recent/planned digital platform for Next Generation investors and a recent Quicken stake.

claims.text: Schwab: On the 3Q25 earnings call (published October 16, 2025), management said 'younger investors at Schwab are highly engaged in building their wealth over the long term.'

Schwab: On the 3Q25 earnings call (published October 16, 2025), management said younger investors are turning to Schwab 'because we have the platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service they need to help them succeed, a combination they cannot find anywhere else.'

Schwab: On the 2Q25 earnings call (published July 18, 2025), management said there is 'no better place to be than here at Schwab' for 'young investors who want to think about how to pay off their college debt, how to buy a house.'

Industry research: Cerulli (published October 29, 2025) states that 'while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.'

Industry research: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) finds that while high-net-worth individuals believe U.S. stocks offer the best opportunities for growing assets, younger investors hold that conviction less strongly.

Industry research: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) states that 'Millennials and Gen Z are increasingly looking beyond the traditional stock and bond markets to build their wealth and are driving demand for everything from investment real estate and private equity to digital assets and gold.'

Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study (published June 17, 2026) reports that 'sixty five percent 65% still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor' among young investors.

Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study (published June 17, 2026) reports that 'eighty seven percent 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios' among young investors.

Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study (published June 17, 2026) reports that Gen Z/Millennials allocate 32% of their portfolio to stocks, compared with 58% for Gen X/Baby Boomers.

Schwab: On the 3Q25 earnings call (published October 16, 2025), management said younger investors' 'top online resource is YouTube, and we're the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.'

Schwab: On the 3Q25 earnings call (published October 16, 2025), management said 'one of the reasons they're turning to Schwab is because we're meeting them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.'

Schwab: On the 2Q26 earnings call (published July 21, 2026), management said 'we've really seen a growth in young investors, I think part of that was started with the removal of commissions, which brought more people into the market that had less money.'
Schwab: On the 3Q25 earnings call (published October 16, 2025), management said 'crypto will be great for clients and will certainly appeal to young investors.'

Schwab: On the 3Q25 earnings call (published October 16, 2025), management said 'younger traders are turning to us because they recognize the potential that trading has in helping build wealth over time.'

Industry research: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) states that 'Millennials and Gen Z Allocate Three Times More of Their Investment Portfolios to Alternative Investments Than Older Generations.'

Industry research: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) reports that among investors ages 21-43, 31% cite real estate investments as a greatest opportunity for growth.

Industry research: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) reports that among investors ages 21-43, 28% cite crypto/digital assets as a greatest opportunity for growth.

Industry research: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) reports that among investors ages 21-43, 26% cite private equity as a greatest opportunity for growth.

Industry research: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) reports that among investors ages 21-43, 24% cite their personal company/brand as a greatest opportunity for growth.

Industry research: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) reports that among investors ages 21-43, 22% cite direct investment into companies as a greatest opportunity for growth.

Industry research: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) reports that among investors ages 21-43, 21% cite companies focused on positive impact as a greatest opportunity for growth.
Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study (published June 17, 2026) reports that 'forty two percent 42% of younger respondents own art.'
Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study (published June 17, 2026) reports that among younger respondents who do not own art, 75% are interested in owning art.
Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study (published June 17, 2026) reports that 'ninety four percent 94% own collectables' among younger respondents.
Schwab: On the 3Q25 earnings call (published October 16, 2025), management said 'we know they learn about finances primarily through social media and family.'

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) describes management targeting 'Next Generation investors' through 'a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.'

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) describes the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer as including 'changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values.'

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) discloses 'a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors' among its client-targeting initiatives.

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) states that the Partnership 'offers a variety of different solutions to clients, including investment advisory programs, brokerage and retirement accounts, cash and lending solutions and financial planning offerings' (general offerings, not specific to younger investors).

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) states that its Digital and Data division 'supports the significant investment in technology infrastructure and digital initiatives to provide new tools for branch teams to better serve clients' (general capability, not specific to younger investors).

Edward Jones: In August 2026, trade press reported that Edward Jones announced it took a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken, as a step toward integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities into Edward Jones to support its value proposition and advisor conversations with clients.
Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) lists among its aspirations to 'attract and serve new client segments.'

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) states Edward Jones aspires to 'anticipate clients' needs with the right offering at the right time, now and for generations to come.'

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) states Edward Jones aspires to 'continue investing in technology to scale our ability to provide financial planning to our clients.'

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) names competition from 'an increasing number of firms of all sizes providing enhanced digital experiences for clients,' including 'artificial intelligence technologies and lower cost, computer-based robo-advice' (competition named generally, not specifically tied to younger investors).

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) names competition from 'fintech' companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms (competition named generally, not specifically tied to younger investors).

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) names competition from 'robo-advisors and other lower cost options,' 'fintech' companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms, and other non-traditional competitors (competition named generally, not specifically tied to younger investors).

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) names competition from 'major competitor brokerage firms that offer zero commissions for purchases and sales of stocks, ETFs and other brokerage products' (competition named generally, not specifically tied to younger investors).

Edward Jones: The 2Q25 10-Q (period ended June 27, 2025, published August 8, 2025) attributes a downward trend in net new assets to higher asset outflows influenced by 'an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm,' among other factors.

Edward Jones: The 3Q25 10-Q (period ended September 26, 2025, published November 7, 2025) states that year-to-date net new asset outflows continue an increasing downward trend influenced by 'an aging client base, generational wealth transfers outside the firm,' and other factors.

Edward Jones: In August 2026, trade press reported that Edward Jones is still determining the actual deployment strategy for Quicken, including where or how it will be offered to clients and integrated into its internal advisor software. Why it might matter: the trade report says clients can be more proactively and productively engaged in the advice process when they have a better understanding of their own financial situation.

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) discloses 'a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors,' part of initiatives including potential future solutions in development and recently launched products. Why it might matter: the 10-K states the success of new initiatives is dependent upon broad adoption by financial advisors, CSTPs and home office associates, and that Edward Jones cannot reliably predict the timing or outcome of the initiatives.

The comparison is not valid on this evidence: the question asks how preferences should shape Edward Jones's offerings, which is normative, and the documents state only what younger investors prefer — Cerulli's finding that younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives, the 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study's figures that 65% of young investors still prefer advice from a human advisor and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI, and Schwab's statement that younger investors need platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service — and what Edward Jones discloses (a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining 'Next Generation investors,' and stated aspirations such as anticipating clients' needs with the right offering at the right time). The two sides are also not on the same basis: the preferences describe young investors generally, while Edward Jones's disclosures describe 'Next Generation investors' and general client segments, and no source states how preferences should shape offerings.

items.text: Schwab says nearly one-third of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Zers, defined as investors ages 13 to 28.

items.text: Schwab says more than 30% of new-to-firm clients are under age 30 and nearly 60% are under age 40.
items.quote: More than 30% of our new-to-firm clients are under the age of 30, and nearly 60% are under the age of 40.

items.quote: 61% Gen Z & Millennial Investors Percent of New Clients 1

items.quote: Our retail business is built to win across generations, wealth tiers, investing styles and engagement preferences... we are well positioned to continue serving future generations when that wealth is passed on.

items.text: Schwab states it improved tax, trust, and estate capabilities and built specialty teams for higher net worth clients.
items.quote: We've improved our tax, trust, and estate capabilities, and we've built out specialty teams catering to the unique needs of our higher net worth clients.

items.text: Schwab is expanding its branch footprint and hiring financial and wealth consultants to deepen relationships with higher net worth retail clients and their families.
items.quote: We're expanding our branch footprint and hiring hundreds of financial consultants and wealth consultants to deepen relationships with our higher net worth retail clients and their families.

a6.SCHW.reason: Passages state Schwab's strategies for capturing wealth: estate planning, tax/trust/estate capabilities, and advisor hiring for higher-net-worth clients and families.

(MS-10K-2025#125), and the supplement says "Advisor‐led client assets represents client assets in accounts that have a Wealth Management representative assigned." (MS-SUPP-2020Q4#3).
claims.source_label: MS supplement 2020-12-31 [IR]; MS 10-K 2025-12-31 [filing]; MS supplement - Wealth Management segment 2020-12-31 [IR]

claims.text: Edward Jones: Client assets per financial advisor is computable on this evidence for the period ended June 26, 2026, whole firm: $2,647 billion in client assets under care at period end divided by 20,514 financial advisors at period end equals $129,033,831 per financial advisor. The inputs are "Client assets under care ($ billions): Total: At period end" of $2,647 billion (EDJ-10Q-2026Q2#59) and financial advisors (actual) of 20,514 at period end (EDJ-10Q-2026Q2#60). A population statement dated 2025-12-31 describes the advisor measure as "Financial advisors (actual): At year end 20,425 20,125 19,232" (EDJ-10K-2025#130).

Raymond James Financial: Client assets per financial advisor is not computable on this evidence, because the two proposed figures cover different populations. The proposed computation cited the financial-advisor count (RJF-10K-2025#9) and client assets under administration (RJF-SUPP-2025Q3#9). The population source states "Advisors in our RCS division are not included in our financial advisor metric although their client assets are included in PCG AUA." (RJF-10K-2025#228).

Morgan Stanley: The January 15, 2026 strategic update deck defines Total Client Assets as "the sum of the reported Wealth Management ('WM') client assets and Investment Management ('IM') assets under management ('AuM')." The definition further states that Wealth Management client assets cover financial advisor-led brokerage, custody, administrative and investment advisory services; self-directed brokerage and investment advisory services; financial and wealth planning services; and workplace services, including stock plan administration and retirement plan services, and that certain Wealth Management client assets are invested in Investment Management products and are also included in Investment Management's AuM.
Morgan Stanley: The 3Q26 supplement (published October 14, 2026) defines advisor-led client assets as "client assets in accounts that have a Wealth Management representative assigned."

Morgan Stanley: The 3Q26 supplement cautions that "These measures are not in accordance with, or a substitute for, U.S. GAAP and may be different from or inconsistent with non-GAAP financial measures used by other companies."

Morgan Stanley: The 3Q26 supplement defines self-directed client assets as active accounts which are not advisor-led, with active accounts defined as having at least $25 in assets; it states "Self-directed client assets represent active accounts which are not advisor-led. Active accounts are defined as having at least $25 in assets."

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K states "The Partnership's more than 20,000 financial advisors ('FA') serve more than 9 million clients with a total of $2.5 trillion in client assets under care as of December 31, 2025."
Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K refers to its advisors as "financial advisors" ("FA").

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K reports its financial advisor count as "financial advisors (actual)" at year end and as an average for the period, shown as "Financial advisors (actual): At year end 20,425 20,125 19,232 1% Average 20,331 19,650 18,945 3%".

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K defines asset-based fee revenue as revenue derived from fees determined by the underlying value of client assets, including advisory programs fees, service fees, and other asset-based fee revenue; it states "Asset-based fee revenue - Revenue is derived from fees determined by the underlying value of client assets and includes advisory programs fees, service fees, and other asset-based fee revenue."

Edward Jones: The 2Q26 10-Q (period ended June 26, 2026) states "The Partnership ended the second quarter of 2026 with $2.6 trillion of assets under care ('AUC'), including $1.2 trillion of advisory programs AUC."
Raymond James Financial: The company's investor-day materials state "The definitions for client assets may be inconsistent across companies."

Raymond James Financial: The 2025 10-K states "Financial advisors associated with firms in RCS are not included in our financial advisor counts, although their client assets are included in our AUA. AUA associated with firms in our RCS division totaled $217.3 billion as of September 30, 2025."

Across the five firms: Client assets per financial advisor cannot be validly compared on this evidence. Only Edward Jones yields a computable figure ($2,647 billion in client assets under care divided by 20,514 financial advisors = $129,033,831, period ended June 26, 2026, whole firm). Morgan Stanley's and Raymond James's proposed computations were rejected because the client-asset and advisor figures cover different populations, Schwab discloses client assets but no financial-advisor headcount, and Merrill discloses no per-advisor figure. The components also are not on a common basis. Advisor headcounts differ: Morgan Stanley reports "Wealth Management representatives" (last found 15,950 at December 31, 2020); Edward Jones reports "financial advisors (actual)"; Raymond James excludes advisors in its RCS division from its financial advisor metric even though their client assets are in AUA; Schwab and Merrill disclose no comparable financial-advisor headcount (Schwab only Form ADV employee counts, Merrill only counts spanning GWIM and Consumer Banking). Client-asset measures differ: Morgan Stanley's "Total Client Assets" is the sum of Wealth Management client assets and Investment Management AuM; Schwab's "client assets" is the market value of assets in its custody, BDA balances, and proprietary products; Edward Jones reports "client assets under care"; Merrill reports "total client balances"; Raymond James reports "client assets under administration". Raymond James's investor-day materials state "The definitions for client assets may be inconsistent across companies." (RJF-DECK-2025-investor-day#32).

a1.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley states that a Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor (MSVA) is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus and does not retain any portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee.
items.quote: If your account is serviced through a Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor ("MSVA"), your MSVA is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus and does not retain any portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee.

a1.MS.reason: The firm discloses a fixed base-salary component for its Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor, a narrower advisor group.

a2.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley states that for certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.
items.quote: For certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.
items.scope: Wealth Management and Investment Management revenue-producing employees

Schwab: A trade press report (published August 20, 2026) quotes a recruiter as saying Schwab pays its W-2 advisors a bonus for winning client assets, in addition to salary.

Edward Jones: In its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025), Edward Jones states that financial advisors may be entitled to additional compensation based on their respective branch office profitability and the profitability of the Partnership.

Merrill: In its Form ADV (published October 30, 2026), Merrill states that advisors who join Merrill from other firms generally receive payments that may include deferred payments, a form of compensation contingent on continued employment, along with salary guarantees, upfront awards and recruitment loans.

Merrill: In its Form ADV (published October 30, 2026), Merrill states that Advisors are eligible to receive a compensation award payable over a defined period of time from an incentive program based on meeting growth targets.

Raymond James Financial: In its Form ADV (published September 14, 2026), Raymond James states that financial incentives for initial/ongoing affiliation with the Firm include deferred compensation arrangements.

Raymond James Financial: In its Form ADV (published September 14, 2026), Raymond James states that qualification for recognition clubs can result in deferred compensation awards to the financial advisor, along with paid travel and reimbursement of certain business-related expenses.

Morgan Stanley: In its 2025 10-K (Item 7), Morgan Stanley states that deferred compensation for financial advisors in the Wealth Management business segment is generally composed of 25% stock-based awards.

Raymond James Financial: In its Form ADV (published September 14, 2026), Raymond James states that financial incentives for affiliation include transition assistance and repayable business transition or working capital loans, among other arrangements.

a1.MER.label: fact

items.text: Merrill's Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf took over in 2023.
items.quote: Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf, who took over in 2023

items.text: Nathan Marsden took over Merrill's Northeast region in June 2023 after running the Mid-America region.
items.quote: Marsden, a 33-year Merrill lifer, took over the Northeast region in June 2023 after running the Mid-America region, according to his LinkedIn profile.

a1.MER.reason: No 2026 leadership-role changes are stated; the passages state 2023 leadership changes, which are facts for their periods.

a2.MER.label: fact

items.text: Merrill returned to veteran broker recruiting and restored a focus on hiring and a more aggressive offer after pulling back at the end of 2017.
items.quote: The firm largely pulled back from veteran broker recruiting at the end of 2017 but returned after Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf, who took over in 2023, restored a focus on hiring and a more aggressive offer.

items.text: Merrill, along with Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo, continues to boost and develop sales of alternative investments and artificial intelligence functions for financial advisors in 2026.
items.quote: Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo , three of the major wirehouses, continue to boost and develop sales of alternative investments , along with artificial intelligence functions , for financial advisors in 2026.

items.text: Merrill signaled it will continue to invest in AI and digital capabilities.
items.quote: While the Merrill executive did not mention new AI tools, the message was clear that the firm would continue to invest in AI and digital capabilities.

a2.MER.reason: Passages state Merrill's strategy priorities: veteran recruiting and continued investment in alternatives, AI, and digital capabilities.

a3.MER.label: different_quantity

items.text: Bank of America had a net loss of 552 advisors in 2026 through Aug. 13, according to Wolfe Research.
items.quote: According to that analysis of regulatory filings, Bank of America had a net loss of 552 advisors, followed by Edward Jones and Equitable Advisors, with 334 each.

items.text: Merrill's ADV reports approximately 26,599 employees are registered representatives of a broker-dealer.
items.quote: (2) Approximately how many of the employees reported in 5.A. are registered representatives of a broker-dealer? 26599

items.text: Merrill's ADV reports approximately 32,960 employees, excluding clerical workers.
items.quote: A. Approximately how many employees do you have? Include full- and part-time employees but do not include any clerical workers. 32960

a3.MER.differs_because: The 552 figure is a net advisor loss for Bank of America (parent), not Merrill alone; the ADV figures are total employees and broker-dealer registered representatives, not a Merrill financial-advisor headcount.
a3.MER.reason: No Merrill-only financial-advisor headcount is stated; only parent-level net advisor loss and ADV employee/registered-rep counts appear.

a4.MER.label: different_quantity

items.text: GWIM reported quarterly net client flows of about $38 billion in Q3 2026, including approximately $20 billion of AUM flows.
items.quote: Quarterly net client flows were about $38 billion, including approximately $20 billion of AUM flows, bringing four-quarter AUM flows to about $74 billion.

items.text: GWIM AUM net client flows were $20,372 million in Q1 2026.
GWIM AUM net client flows were $13,673 million in Q2 2026.
GWIM AUM net client flows were $19,980 million in Q3 2026.

a4.MER.differs_because: Figures are for the Global Wealth & Investment Management segment (Merrill Wealth Management plus Bank of America Private Bank), not Merrill alone.
a4.MER.reason: No Merrill-only net new asset flows are stated; GWIM segment net client flows are the closest, wider measure.

a5.MER.label: fact

items.text: Merrill Wealth Management client balances were $3,992,312 million at December 31, 2025.
Merrill Wealth Management client balances were $3,815,389 million at March 31, 2026.
Merrill Wealth Management client balances were $4,132,451 million at June 30, 2026.
Merrill Wealth Management client balances were $4,240,601 million at September 30, 2026.

a5.MER.reason: Merrill Wealth Management client balances are stated at each quarter-end since the start of the year.

a6.MER.label: fact

items.text: Merrill announced the launch of Tax Efficient Transition Service (TET) and Dollar Cost Averaging Service (DCA) in September 2026.
items.quote: Merrill today announced the launch of Tax Efficient Transition Service (TET) and Dollar Cost Averaging Service (DCA), new services that combine automation with professional portfolio oversight to help clients simplify asset transitions and cash deployment into managed or custom managed investment strategies in the Merrill Lynch Investment Advisory Program (IAP).

a6.MER.reason: The passage states a new product/service launch at Merrill.

a7.MER.label: fact

items.text: Merrill newly created two kinds of fees for third-party managers—data analytics fees and a revenue-sharing support fee—effective Jan. 1, 2027.
items.quote: Two kinds of fees have been newly created. Third-party managers can buy as much as $1.4 million worth of 'incentives' per annum through one fee, by maxing out data analytics buys. The second fee is a basis points revenue share that can cost asset managers as much as 0.1% on all Merill assets they manage.

items.text: Merrill's new data analytics fees for actively managed products will cost asset managers between $125,000 and $860,000 per firm per year.
items.quote: Merrill's new data analytics fees will cost asset managers between $125,000 and $860,000 per-firm, per-year for data on actively managed products, including ETFs, mutual funds, annuities and model portfolios.

items.text: Data on passive ETFs managed through Merrill's platforms will cost between $25,000 and $550,000.
items.quote: Data on passive ETFs managed through Merrill's platforms will cost between $25,000 and $550,000.

items.text: Merrill's new negotiable revenue-sharing 'support fee' will cost up to $1 million for every $1 billion of funds an asset manager manages on behalf of Merrill advisors, with fees from 0.02% to a maximum 0.1%.
items.quote: Its new 'negotiable' revenue-sharing 'support fee' will cost up to $1 million, for every $1 billion of funds an asset manager manages on behalf of Merrill advisors, with fees ranging from 0.02% on high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth assets, to a maximum 0.1% on third party mutual funds, money market funds, and active ETFs.

items.text: TET and DCA are optional with no additional IAP Program Fees charged.
items.quote: Both services are optional and available to clients, with no additional IAP Program Fees charged.

a7.MER.reason: Passages state Merrill's new fees for third-party managers and a no-additional-fee statement for new services.

a8.MER.label: fact

items.text: Merrill says broker incentives will not shift under the new third-party data and support fees.
items.quote: The fees will give third parties a leg up over competing third parties that decline to pay, but broker incentives will not shift, the company says.

items.text: Merrill restored a focus on hiring and a more aggressive recruiting offer after pulling back from veteran broker recruiting at the end of 2017.
items.quote: The firm largely pulled back from veteran broker recruiting at the end of 2017 but returned after Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf, who took over in 2023, restored a focus on hiring and a more aggressive offer.

a8.MER.reason: Passages state broker incentives will not shift and that Merrill restored a more aggressive recruiting offer.

a9.MER.label: not_found
a9.MER.reason: No passages state Merrill branch office openings, closings, or footprint changes.

a10.MER.label: fact

items.text: Merrill signaled it will continue to invest in AI and digital capabilities.
items.quote: While the Merrill executive did not mention new AI tools, the message was clear that the firm would continue to invest in AI and digital capabilities.

items.text: GWIM cites new AI-enabled tools that help advisers prepare for client conversations, identify opportunities, and deliver more personalized advice at scale.
items.quote: Franchise continued to benefit from strong adviser productivity, growing digital engagement and new AI-enabled tools that help advisers prepare for client conversations, identify opportunities and deliver more personalized advice at scale.

a10.MER.reason: Passages state continued investment in AI/digital capabilities and new AI-enabled tools.

a11.MER.label: fact

items.text: Merrill faces restitution of approximately $549,000 in excess commissions in a settlement with state securities regulators over unreasonable commissions.
items.quote: Merrill Lynch faces restitution on approximately $549,000 in excess commissions over the same period, NASAA said.

items.text: As a condition of the settlement, the firms must certify that their commission policies and supervisory procedures have been revised.
items.quote: As a condition of the settlement, the firms must certify that their commission policies and supervisory procedures have been revised to ensure all charges are fair and reasonable going forward.

items.text: Merrill agreed to pay $39 million to settle a class action lawsuit over interest rates paid on cash in retirement accounts.
items.quote: Merrill to pay $39 ​million to settle a class action lawsuit that alleged it paid brokerage clients close-to-zero ‌interest rates instead of market rates on cash in retirement accounts.

items.text: A Merrill spokesperson said the firm addressed the issues raised in the commission settlement several years ago and is pleased to have reached a resolution.
items.quote: a Merrill spokesperson said the firm "addressed the issues raised in the settlement several years ago and is pleased to have reached a resolution with the states"

a11.MER.reason: Passages state Merrill's regulatory settlements and required compliance revisions.

a12.MER.label: fact

Merrill Wealth Management revenue was $5,579 million in Q1 2026.

claims.text: Edward Jones: The 3Q25 10-Q (period ended September 26, 2025) reported financial advisor attrition of 6.1% for the third quarter of 2025, defining "Attrition %" as "the annualized number of financial advisors that left or retired from the Partnership during the period compared to the total number of financial advisors as of period end." The 10-Q states: "The Partnership ended the third quarter with 20,429 financial advisors. Financial advisor attrition was 6.1% as a result of a variety of factors, including a rise in financial advisor departures with tenure of five years or less."

Edward Jones: The 2Q25 10-Q (period ended June 27, 2025) reported that financial advisor attrition increased to 6.4% in the second quarter of 2025, "primarily due to an increase in retirements, consistent with industry trends." The 10-Q states: "The Partnership ended the second quarter with 20,309 financial advisors. Financial advisor attrition increased to 6.4% primarily due to an increase in retirements, consistent with industry trends."

Edward Jones: The 3Q25 10-Q (period ended September 26, 2025) reported financial advisor attrition of 4.7% for the third quarter of 2024, in a table row reading "Attrition %(5) 6.1% 4.7% 30% 6.0% 5.1% 18%".

Edward Jones: The 3Q25 10-Q (period ended September 26, 2025) reported financial advisor attrition of 6.0% for the nine months ended September 26, 2025, in a table row reading "Attrition %(5) 6.1% 4.7% 30% 6.0% 5.1% 18%".

Edward Jones: The 3Q25 10-Q (period ended September 26, 2025) reported financial advisor attrition of 5.1% for the nine months ended September 27, 2024, in a table row reading "Attrition %(5) 6.1% 4.7% 30% 6.0% 5.1% 18%".

Merrill: On the 2Q26 Bank of America earnings call (transcript published July 14, 2026), CFO Alastair Borthwick said Merrill's "adviser attrition is now at near historic lows. So we're pretty happy with that." The passage states no numeric attrition rate.

Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025, published March 13, 2026) states: "The Partnership experiences continued efforts by competing firms to hire away its financial advisors, although the Partnership believes its rate of attrition of financial advisors is in line with comparable firms."

A numeric comparison of the two firms' financial advisor attrition rates, or of either rate against an industry attrition rate, is not valid on this evidence. Edward Jones discloses an annualized attrition rate — 6.1% for the third quarter of 2025 and 6.4% for the second quarter of 2025, defined as "the annualized number of financial advisors that left or retired from the Partnership during the period compared to the total number of financial advisors as of period end" — but Merrill discloses no attrition rate number; the only Merrill item is Bank of America CFO Alastair Borthwick's 2Q26 statement that "adviser attrition is now at near historic lows." The industry research figures are not an attrition rate either: they measure advisors' self-reported likelihood of leaving their employer within the next 12 months (Struggling advisors 4X as likely as Thriving; nearly 1 in 10 Struggling extremely likely; 1 in 50 Thriving extremely likely). Edward Jones itself offers only a qualitative comparison, stating in its 2025 10-K that the Partnership "believes its rate of attrition of financial advisors is in line with comparable firms," and in its 2Q25 10-Q that the 6.4% increase was "consistent with industry trends."

items.text: Morgan Stanley states that for certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.
items.quote: For certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.
items.scope: Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments

items.text: Morgan Stanley said it will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation, supporting its overall investment into its financial advisors and simplifying its compensation program.
items.quote: we will also increase the cash component of our advisor compensation. We are making these changes to reduce the accounting-driven volatility in revenues and earnings.

items.text: Morgan Stanley stated that in the first quarter of 2026, the Firm reduced the amount of deferred compensation as a proportion of total compensation for Wealth Management advisors.
items.quote: Additionally, in the first quarter of 2026, the Firm reduced the amount of deferred compensation as a proportion of total compensation for Wealth Management advisors.

items.text: Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year.
items.quote: As it has in the past, Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year.

items.text: Morgan Stanley for years has taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue, called it deferred compensation, and required advisors to stay for years in order to vest.
items.quote: Giants like Morgan Stanley for years have taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue, called it deferred compensation, and required advisors to stay for years in order to vest.

items.text: Morgan Stanley is not introducing retention bonuses as part of its 2027 pay plans for advisors, adhering to a more traditional approach.
items.quote: Morgan Stanley and Merrill Lynch are not introducing retention bonuses as part of their 2027 pay plans for advisors, adhering to a more traditional approach.

On the 4Q 2025 earnings call (published January 15, 2026), management said that in the first quarter of 2026, in its words, "we will also increase the cash component of our advisor compensation. We are making these changes to reduce the accounting-driven volatility in revenues and earnings," supporting its overall investment into its financial advisors and simplifying its compensation program.

Morgan Stanley's 2Q 2026 Form 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2026, Item 2) states: "Additionally, in the first quarter of 2026, the Firm reduced the amount of deferred compensation as a proportion of total compensation for Wealth Management advisors."

Trade press reports (published October 26, 2026) that "As it has in the past, Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year."

Trade press reports (published October 26, 2026) that Morgan Stanley for years has taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue, called it deferred compensation, and required advisors to stay for years in order to vest.

Trade press reports (published October 26, 2026) that "Morgan Stanley and Merrill Lynch are not introducing retention bonuses as part of their 2027 pay plans for advisors, adhering to a more traditional approach."
